title: A conference, a castle, and a very convenient pool.
summary: A Gaylord Palms Fiber Connect conference, Disney’s Pop Century stay, a Skyliner ride and a Crystal Palace meal—with original photos and practical Orlando travel notes.
search: The journal/Travel · Orlando, Florida Fiber Connect, with the Graphical Networks team.A working trip, with a little room for wonderA conference, a castle, and a very convenient pool.Fiber Connect brought me to Florida. Staying at Disney gave the hours around work a little extra charm.Published October 6, 2026 Work: Fiber ConnectStay: Pop CenturyFlight: JetBlueMap & placesPractical tipsPrint a planning list There are work trips where the hotel is simply where you leave your suitcase. On this one, I stayed at Disney’s Pop Century Resort—and the pool was right outside my room.An excellent detail. Possibly the detail I should lead with.I flew JetBlue to Florida for Fiber Connect with Graphical Networks. The conference took place at the beautiful Gaylord Palms Resort & Convention Center, while Pop Century was my home base. Around the work came a lovely Skyliner ride, the Crystal Palace buffet, and a little time at Disney.Michael and James stayed home. The Evil Queen, however, made an appearance. ;) A little Magic Kingdom time around the work schedule.A Disney address for a working tripThe pleasure of being close.Gaylord Palms was a lovely setting for the conference. Staying at Pop Century gave the trip another atmosphere altogether: bright, playful, and unmistakably Disney.And then there was that pool. Having it right outside my room was such a pleasure. After a day of work, I appreciated being close to something enjoyable without having to organize another outing.Even when James isn’t traveling with me, I notice those practical details. How far is the walk? How easily could we return to the room? Is the thing we would most enjoy conveniently nearby?Those questions matter just as much to me as a hotel’s photographs. The journey gets a place in the storyThe Skyliner was part of the pleasure.I loved the Skyliner ride. Transportation can feel like something to get through, but this was a lovely part of the trip itself.Pop Century is connected through the Skyliner network to EPCOT and Disney’s Hollywood Studios. It is worth looking at the route and current operating information before building the day around it.My own takeaway was simpler: leave time to enjoy the ride.Official Skyliner routes and operating updates →Original editorial illustration. The bright dining room, the buffet, and a visit from Eeyore made a memorable combination.I still found myself thinking about how the experience might work for our family. Being able to see food before choosing it can be useful. So can knowing beforehand that characters may approach the table.For a future visit with James, I would look at the current food choices, preview the setting, and plan around what felt comfortable for him. This was my trip, so those are considerations for another visit—not things I tested with him.Crystal Palace is inside Magic Kingdom. Disney recommends reservations; valid park admission is also required, and a park reservation may be needed depending on the ticket. title: Before you go.
summary: Practical notes to copy and adapt before an outing, school meeting or everyday plan. Clear questions, useful wording and details worth checking.
search: The original practical notesBefore you go.The questions to ask. The words to borrow.Open just the note you need. Copy it, edit it for your situation and keep personal information limited to what is useful. The practical detailsQuestions to ask and notes to borrow. Open whatever you need. Plan a day out Seven questions before you go A little more information before leaving the house can save a lot of guessing when you get there. When is it quieter?Ask about crowds, music, hand dryers, and scheduled events. Where can we take a break?Check for a calm space and whether you can leave and re-enter. What are the bathrooms like?Ask about privacy, space, and the specific facilities you need. What can we bring?Confirm food, drinks, communication devices, and familiar comfort items. How does the visit actually work?Check queues, parking distance, steps, seating, and any required waiting. Is the main attraction open?Confirm today's availability, hours, age rules, and access restrictions. What happens if plans change?Ask about cancellation, refunds, and a shorter visit before booking. ShareCopyPrint Ask for access A clear request can be short. Explain what gets in the way, say what would help, and ask for a reply in writing. A note you can borrow Hi, we're planning to visit [place] on [date]. A family member has a disability, and [barrier] makes it difficult to take part. Would it be possible to [specific adjustment]? Please let us know what you can arrange and who to ask for when we arrive. If that won't work, is there another option? A written reply would help us plan. Thank you! Copy this request Be specificCould we wait somewhere quieter until it's our turn?Could you send a few photos or tell us what happens during the visit?Can our support person stay with us?Could we have the instructions in writing too? You can begin with the access need. Your family's entire history needn't go into the first email. US guidance: businesses open to the public and effective communication. Duties and exceptions depend on the setting. This is a starting point for a request, not individual legal advice. Hotels and pools A lovely lobby is a bonus. A working pool and the right beds are rather more important. The room: what are the actual beds? Does the separate sleeping area have a door? “Suite” leaves a surprising amount unanswered.The pool: is it open on your dates? And the hot tub? Ask about hours, age rules, and water temperature if it matters to you.The timing: can you swim before check-in or after checkout?The food: what exactly is in the kitchenette? A fridge and microwave won't do the same job as a stove.The noise: ask about events, room location, and somewhere to take a quiet break.The bill: get the total with taxes, parking, fees, and deposits. Read the cancellation terms before paying. Hi, we're looking at a stay on [dates]. Could you confirm the beds and room layout, what's in the kitchenette, and whether both the indoor pool and hot tub will be open? We'd also like their hours and age rules, and whether we can use them before check-in or after checkout. Please include the total with mandatory fees, any deposit, and the cancellation terms. We also need [access adjustment]. Thanks so much! Copy the hotel questions Ask the property about your actual dates. An old pool photograph can only tell you so much. Support communication Please speak to the person. Give them time to answer. Those two things are a very good place to start. AAC means augmentative and alternative communication. Speech, vocalizations, gestures, signs, photographs, objects, writing, spelling, eye gaze, switches, low-tech boards and speech-generating devices can all be part of one multimodal system. Keep the person's communication method within reach. Ask before moving or touching a device.Leave time for a response before asking the question again.Offer choices the person can use, including “no,” “stop,” and “break.”Use language that respects their age. Speech alone doesn't tell you what someone understands. A note for a hostPlease speak directly to our family member and give them time to respond. They communicate using [method]. Please keep it available and ask before touching their device. It helps to [individual preference]. They may also need time to pause. Thank you for making room for this. Copy the communication note Read the full multimodal communication guide → Further reading: CommunicationFIRST, its guidance written by AAC users, and ASAN on autism. Understand ableism Ableism can show up in an ordinary exchange: talking over someone, dismissing an access request, or assuming a person won't enjoy an activity because they need help with it. Some autistic people need substantial support throughout their lives. They still have preferences, privacy, and every reason to be included. What that means hereInclude the person in the conversation.Speak to them, with the communication support they use.Allow a different sort of visit.A break, a shorter stay, or watching before joining in can make the day work.Keep support available.Comfort and communication shouldn't have to be earned.Let private moments stay private.A hard day doesn't need to become a public story. We write as a family. Autistic people speak for themselves, including through AAC, and their own words matter. ASAN on autism · CommunicationFIRST's wording guide If an access request is refused Ask for the reason in writing. It gives you something specific to respond to. Restate the barrier and the adjustment you asked for.Ask which policy applies, and whether another arrangement would work.Find out who can review the decision.Keep the dates and messages. Write down what happened while it's fresh. Thank you for getting back to us. The difficulty is [barrier], and we asked for [adjustment]. Could you explain why that isn't possible, share the relevant policy, and let us know whether an alternative would work? Who could review the request? We'd appreciate a written reply. Copy the follow-up For US rights guidance: businesses, government programs, and Massachusetts communication access. The rules depend on the setting; a refusal alone doesn't establish a legal violation. Make the day simpler One good thing is plentyPick the part of the day everyone is looking forward to. Leave space around it, and know what the shorter version looks like. Before the shoes go onConfirm the hours, parking, bathrooms, and food.Show what comes first, next, and afterward in a familiar way. Actual photos can help.Know where you can take a break, and how to get back to the car. For the bagA communication device and charger, familiar food and drink, a comfort item, spare clothes if needed, and the supplies in the person's usual support plan.There is no prize for staying longer than everyone wants to. Choices, routines & things to do Today's choices, pleaseA choice board needs to match what's actually available. For an ice-cream stop, that means today's flavors at the right shop.Offer a few clear choices, with words and useful pictures.Keep flavor, cone or cup, and size as separate decisions.A strawberry picture says more than a pink square.Include “something else,” “no,” and “finished.” Allow time to choose. A short plan for a new placeShow the place, who will be there, what happens, where a break can happen, and going home. Use real photos when you can. Leave room for things to change. Activities for teensStart with what interests them: swimming, animals, films, a walk, or making something to eat. The amount of help someone needs doesn't make their interests younger.Ask about group size, noise, pace, and whether a support person can join.Check the changing facilities and where to take a break.See whether a short introduction or trial visit is possible.Find a part of the activity they can choose and take part in, with the help they need. A note to hand overThe plan today is [activity and time]. Communication: [method and response time]. What helps: [specific support]. A break: [place or cue]. If plans change: [how to explain or contact us]. Please follow the existing support and emergency plans.Copy the handover note Share private care details securely with the people who need them. More on communication support. Clothes that feel right A beautiful sweater that nobody wants to wear is still a sweater sitting in a drawer.Start with the clothes that feel right. Then look at the details: the collar, the seams, the waistband, and whether the fastenings are manageable.Use measurements. One brand's medium isn't every brand's medium.Check washing and drying before buying.Build around a comfortable shape or color that already gets worn.Read the return policy, especially when ordering an unfamiliar fabric.Classic can be quite simple. Comfortable clothes, a useful layer, and no argument with the waistband.Build a useful wardrobe One family. Not the whole spectrum.We write about what we wear, where we go, what earns space in the house, and the practical side of life with profound autism. The point is not perfection. It is knowing enough to make a better choice before spending the money or loading the car.Our family experience includes profound autism and very high support needs. That gives us one specific lens - not ownership of autism, neurodiversity, or anybody else's story.What that means hereWe use profound autism descriptively for our family's support-needs reality. We know the term is contested. Some families and researchers find it useful; some autistic self-advocates strongly oppose it. We do not use it as a hierarchy of human worth.When we write generally, we usually use identity-first language such as autistic person, while respecting individual preferences when they are known. We welcome autistic and neurodivergent readers across support levels.Some details stay within our family. Useful does not require invasive.Read our language & representation standard Notes from New England A swim and a good lunchGive us somewhere to swim and something good to eat, and there is the beginning of a day out.It is tempting to add three more stops because they're nearby. They will still be there another day. Leave time to enjoy the thing you came for.Before leaving, check the opening hours, food, bathrooms, and somewhere to take a break. Keep a shorter version of the day in mind too.The questions to ask first The unglamorous questionsCan it go in the washing machine? Does the lid come apart for cleaning? Will it need a subscription after we've bought it?Those questions aren't much use in a beautiful photograph. They're rather useful once the parcel arrives.The same goes for meal kits. “Quick” can mean very different things once you count the chopping, extra ingredients, and washing up.The questions we ask before buying A shorter visitThere is a great deal of advice about making the most of a visit. Sometimes that means leaving while everyone is still having a good time.Watching for a while, doing one part, taking a break, or choosing to go home are all things a plan can allow for. Ask about re-entry before you need it.The person taking part should have a say in what comes next. title: Halloween, farm style.
summary: Skeleton glasses, corn sifting, a farm ride and memories of Connor’s Halloween Party at Frerichs Farm in Warren, Rhode Island.
search: The journalWarren, Rhode IslandA Halloween family field note Skeleton glasses. Cookie in hand. Not a bad way to start a Halloween story.A family afternoon at Frerichs FarmHalloween, farm style.A cookie, some spectacular skeleton glasses, corn to sift—and a farm that made a special Halloween invitation to autistic families.An AUsome Life · Published October 7, 2026 From an earlier family visitSome photographs bring back a whole afternoon. These are the ones with a yellow Black Panther shirt, a bit of Halloween mischief, and the three of us sitting close together in the October sunshine.They were taken at Frerichs Farm in Warren, Rhode Island. They still make me smile. Our afternoonConnor’s Halloween PartyThe farm ride More photographsMap & visit detailsAccess & sensory notes Opened from the family albumA little skeleton and a lot of personality.The Halloween glasses deserve their own place in the album. White plastic bones frame a tiny skull, held up in front of one eye. A cookie is being kept very firmly in the other hand. The shirt is bright yellow, and absolutely none of the photograph looks like it needed organizing by an adult.Behind him, people are sitting under a big tent. The grass is green, the light is lovely, and it is the kind of unplanned photograph that ends up meaning more than the ones we spend ten minutes trying to pose.For us, these little moments are the story. Not how many attractions we did, or how much we fitted into an afternoon. Just the part we actually enjoyed. Pour, sift, watch, repeat. A good activity does not have to hurry.All three of us together in the autumn sun. A small activity, a real memoryThere was a table full of sand and corn.The sifting station was a wonderfully simple thing: a shallow tabletop, scattered corn kernels, a wooden screen, and a paper cup for pouring. It offered something to do with your hands and something interesting to watch happen.I love that we kept a picture of it. Sometimes the most absorbing stop of the day is not the grand attraction. It is an ordinary little activity that makes sense immediately, with no instructions required. A small study in autumn. Original editorial illustration.The invitation that matteredConnor’s Halloween Party.Frerichs Farm has hosted a special gathering called Connor’s Halloween Party, created for people on the autism spectrum and their families. It has been offered free of charge, with an RSVP, as a chance for families to enjoy some autumn fun together.That intention is part of why I wanted this farm in our family journal. A place can have pumpkins, wagons, treats and games, but there is something extra meaningful about an event that deliberately says to families like ours: this day is for you, too.Previous descriptions of the party mention activities such as the Western Town, pirate ship, bubbles, a scavenger hunt, a bouncy house and food. Activities can change by year, and a designated autism event is not a guarantee that every sound, surface or crowd will suit every person. Still, the invitation itself matters.A note on dates: Despite being a memory from an earlier visit, this is not necessarily a discontinued event. Frerichs Farm listed Connor’s Halloween for October 3, 2026 (rain date October 4). That date has passed; check the farm’s official party page and calendar for any future celebration and RSVP details. In the middle of it allThree of us, a patch of sun.We took several family selfies, and not one needed to be perfect. In one, our son looks away from the camera. In another, he turns toward us. The sun makes its own plans.We were there together. That is the picture I wanted to keep.The bright orange railings behind us, the blue jackets, the rows of white tents in the distance—those details make this feel like a specific day, not just a generic autumn outing.A second photograph from the same few sunny minutes. Little pieces of the dayThe camera kept rolling.There are a few short videos from the farm ride, too: a look at the tractor, an orange railing against the sky, and the happy disorder of everybody trying to get a view. I am keeping them here with the photographs, because sometimes a moving picture brings the whole place back. title: Get in the photograph.
summary: For the mother who plans the outing and takes the pictures: a reminder to get in the photograph, with a moment from our own family album.
search: The journal / Family life Motherhood · From the family album Get in the photograph. For the mother who plans the outing, packs the bag, and takes the pictures: make sure there are some with you in them, too. October 16, 2026 Arms in the air. A moment from our family album. I love this one of James and me. Arms in the air, a grey New England sky, a little silliness beside the water. This is part of motherhood I want to remember: enjoying each other’s company. Hand someone the phone. Ask for a few pictures. You don’t have to arrange everyone, put away the familiar things, or wait for matching smiles. Leave room for the moment as it is. And when you look through them, give yourself a little kindness. Keep the one that makes you remember being there together. You belong in the family album. More on motherhood →Back to the journal →
